paper_context.research_question: Can unannotated Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) system outputs be automatically annotated with linguistically-informed edit spans and dataset-independent error types so that per-error-type evaluation of GEC systems becomes possible and reliable?
main_claims: A linguistically-enhanced alignment combined with a rule-based, dataset-independent classifier can automatically extract edits and assign error types to unannotated GEC system output.
Human experts judged the predicted error types as 'Good' or 'Acceptable' for at least ~95% of sampled edits, indicating high qualitative appropriateness of the automatic labels.
Reprocessing gold references with the same automatic alignment/classification pipeline yields results not statistically different from using gold annotations, validating the auto-annotation approach.

The resulting annotations enable the first detailed per-error-type evaluation of all systems in the CoNLL-2014 shared task, revealing complementary strengths/weaknesses across systems (e.g., MT better at multi-token edits; classifiers better at some verb-form categories).
The tool (to be released) facilitates standardized error-type evaluation and separates edit extraction from evaluation, reducing artefacts introduced by scorers like M2.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Annotation quality: human judgment distribution (Good/Acceptable/Bad) and inter-annotator agreement (κfree).
Alignment/extraction accuracy: how well automatic edit spans correspond to human edits (precision/recall/F1 approximations reported elsewhere and referenced).
Classifier correctness per error category: proportion of correctly assigned categories across 25+ types (measured via manual rating).
Robustness across datasets: applicability to CoNLL-2014 and FCE-test and independence from dataset-specific labels.
Impact on system evaluation: comparison of scores using auto-annotated vs. gold references (statistical significance via bootstrap).
Granularity & consistency: ability to evaluate at operation tier (Missing/Replacement/Unnecessary), POS-based categories, multi-token edits, and detection vs. correction.
Tool transparency and determinism: interpretability of rules and reproducibility of annotations.

extracted_claims.claim_text: A linguistically-enhanced alignment combined with a rule-based, dataset-independent classifier can automatically extract edits and assign error types to unannotated GEC system output.
evidence: Abstract: "using a linguistically-enhanced alignment to automatically extract the edits... and then classify them using a new dataset-independent rule-based classifier."
Sec. 2: describes use of Felice et al. (2016) linguistically-enhanced Damerau-Levenshtein alignment and merging rules for edit extraction.
Sec. 3: describes rule-based classifier using automatic POS, lemmas, stemming, dependency parses and Hunspell for non-word detection.
uncertainty_flags: Extent to which alignment errors (boundary mistakes, merges/splits) degrade downstream classification is described qualitatively but not fully quantified in this paper.
Details of the full rule set and edge-case handling are not fully listed in main text (Appendix A lists valid combinations but not all rules).

extracted_claims.claim_text: Human experts judged the predicted error types as 'Good' or 'Acceptable' for at least ~95% of sampled edits, indicating high qualitative appropriateness of the automatic labels.
evidence: Sec. 3.3: "we asked 5 GEC researchers to rate... 200 randomly chosen edits... as 'Good', 'Acceptable' or 'Bad'."
Table 3: per-rater distributions; overall 86.3% Good, 10.0% Acceptable, 3.7% Bad; text: "all 5 raters individually considered at least 95%... to be either 'Good' or 'Acceptable'."
uncertainty_flags: Apparent discrepancy between per-rater individual >=95% statement and aggregated table (overall 96.3% Good+Acceptable) — needs verification of whether per-rater >=95% holds for each rater.
Small sample size (200 edits) and only 5 expert raters; representativeness across all 25+ error types and across datasets may be limited.
Raters were instructed to ignore boundary quality; hence ratings measure label appropriateness conditional on extracted spans, not end-to-end correctness.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Auto-annotated references equivalent to gold for scoring
extracted_claims.claim_text: Reprocessing gold references with the same automatic alignment/classification pipeline yields results not statistically different from using original gold annotations, validating the auto-annotation approach for evaluation.
extracted_claims.section_anchor: Sec. 4.1 (Gold Reference vs. Auto Reference); Table 4
evidence: Sec. 4.1: authors reprocessed reference files automatically and compared scores using M2 and their edit-comparison method.

Table 4: shows team scores under gold vs auto references with both M2 and their approach; text states bootstrap significance testing (1,000 iterations) found no statistically significant difference (p > .05).
uncertainty_flags: Bootstrap test details are brief: exact statistic tested, confidence intervals, and which comparisons passed are not fully tabulated in the paper.
Reprocessing discards some human annotation structure; equivalence observed for aggregate scores but may hide per-category mismatches.
Potential dependence on particular datasets (CoNLL-2014); robustness to other corpora asserted but limited evidence presented.

extracted_claims.claim_text: The resulting annotations enable detailed per-error-type evaluation of all systems in the CoNLL-2014 shared task, revealing complementary strengths/weaknesses across systems (e.g., MT better at multi-token edits; classifiers better at some verb-form categories).
extracted_claims.section_anchor: Sec. 4 (CoNLL-2014 Shared Task Analysis); Secs. 4.2–4.6; Tables 5–8; Table 6
evidence: Sec. 4: pipeline applied to CoNLL-2014 system outputs to produce annotated hypothesis files.
Tables 5 and 6: show precision, recall, F0.5 per team for operation tiers and 24+ error categories.
Sec. 4.5: Table 8 shows multi-token edit performance; observations that MT-based systems achieved higher multi-token scores.
uncertainty_flags: Validity of per-error-type comparisons depends on correctness of edit span extraction and classification for each category; per-category error rates of annotation not independently reported.
Some systems did not attempt certain error types (dashes in tables), complicating comparisons.
Observed patterns might reflect dataset-specific system tuning; generalizability to other corpora is asserted but limitedly demonstrated.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Tool separates extraction from evaluation and reduces scorer artefacts
extracted_claims.claim_text: Treating edit extraction and evaluation as separate tasks and annotating both hypotheses and references in the same format reduces artefacts introduced by scorers like M2 and facilitates straightforward F-score comparison of edits.
evidence: Sec. 4: describes how annotating both files enables simple TP/FP/FN counting based on identical spans+corrections.
Sec. 4.1: discusses how M2 merges/splits edits and can inflate scores; author argues their approach avoids scorer's dynamic boundary exploitation.
uncertainty_flags: Claim that M2 'overestimates' performance is supported by qualitative examples and references but not exhaustively quantified for all cases.
Separating extraction and evaluation introduces dependence on the chosen extraction algorithm; different extractors could produce different evaluation artefacts.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The Felice et al. (2016) linguistically-enhanced alignment algorithm (with merging rules) reliably approximates human edit spans across datasets used (CoNLL-2014, FCE-test) with ~80-85 F1.
supporting_evidence: Sec. 2: cites Felice et al. (2016) and reports "proved most effective at approximating human edits in several datasets (80-85 F1)".
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If alignment quality is lower on certain edit types or systems, extracted spans will be incorrect leading to wrong classification and misleading per-error-type evaluation.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Automatic linguistic markup (spaCy POS, lemmas, dependency parses, Lancaster stemmer, Hunspell) is sufficiently accurate for the rule-based classifier to assign correct error types in most cases.
supporting_evidence: Sec. 3.1: lists spaCy v1.6 for tagging/lemmatization/dep parsing, Lancaster stemmer, and Hunspell for non-word detection.
Sec. 3.3: when 'Bad' ratings occurred, they were often attributable to POS tagger mistakes.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Systematic tagging errors (esp. on learner language) can produce systematic misclassification of error types; reported high human-rated quality may overstate classifier correctness if tagger fails on specific categories.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Manual evaluation of 200 edits by 5 GEC researchers is representative enough to validate the classifier across its full set of 25+ error types.
supporting_evidence: Sec. 3.3: 200 randomly chosen edits (100 FCE-test, 100 CoNLL-2014) rated by 5 experts.
Table 3: aggregated ratings and κfree reported.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the sample under-represents rare or difficult error types, classifier limitations in those categories will be unobserved, leading to overconfidence in dataset-independent claims.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Reprocessing gold references with the automatic pipeline produces annotation files that are comparable to original gold annotations for the purpose of system-level scoring.
supporting_evidence: Sec. 4.1: authors reprocessed references and report no significant differences in scores (bootstrap, p>.05).
Table 4: shows gold vs auto reference scores for teams under M2 and their approach.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If reprocessing changes reference edits in ways that affect specific error-type tallies or certain systems, comparative conclusions about system strengths may be biased.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: F0.5 and precision/recall computed over auto-annotated edits provide meaningful comparisons between systems and error categories.
supporting_evidence: Many tables present P/R/F0.5 per team per category and per operation tier; authors interpret these to compare system behaviors.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If error-class assignment or span matching errors differ systematically across systems (e.g., some systems produce edits that the extractor tends to split/merge), P/R/F0.5 comparisons could reflect extractor artefacts rather than true system differences.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Dataset-independence of the rule-based classifier generalizes beyond CoNLL-2014 and FCE-test because classification uses only automatic properties (POS, lemma, token ops).
supporting_evidence: Sec. 3 argues approach is dataset-independent and analogous to automating human annotator guidelines; relies solely on automatic mark-up.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If different datasets exhibit different error distributions or annotation conventions that interact with automatic markup (e.g., tokenization differences), classifier outputs may be less comparable across datasets.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Bootstrap significance test (1,000 iterations) with p > .05 is an adequate method to conclude no significant difference between auto and gold references.
supporting_evidence: Sec. 4.1: authors state they validated with bootstrap testing (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993), 1,000 iterations, p > .05.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the tested statistic, resampling method, or multiple comparisons correction are inadequate, the non-significance finding may be unreliable; specific per-category differences might be masked.

argument_focus: Feasibility and reliability of automatic edit extraction and dataset-independent rule-based classification for GEC outputs.
Use of auto-annotated references to enable per-error-type evaluation and comparison across systems.
Claimed qualitative parity between auto-annotated and human gold references for system-level scoring.
contribution_targets: A rule-based, dataset-independent error-type classifier operating on automatic linguistic annotations (Sec. 3).
A pipeline combining linguistically-enhanced alignment (Felice et al., 2016) and the classifier to auto-annotate hypothesis and reference files (Secs. 2–4).
A data product: annotated CoNLL-2014 system outputs enabling per-error-type analyses (Sec. 4 and Tables).
A proposed evaluation workflow that separates edit extraction from scoring to avoid M2 scorer artefacts (Sec. 4.1).
evaluation_targets: Quality of edit extraction: alignment boundary accuracy, merge/split behavior, per-error-type extraction error rates (related to Sec. 2 claims).
Classifier correctness per error category: proportion correct per category (beyond the 200-edit manual sample), and error patterns linked to POS/tagging failures (Sec. 3.3).
Robustness of auto-annotated references vs gold: detailed per-category statistical comparisons, not only aggregate F-scores (Sec. 4.1).
Impact of automatic markup errors (POS/lemma/dep/tagging) on downstream classification and system rankings (Sec. 3.1 & 3.3).
Effect of extraction decisions on multi-token edits and example-driven cases where M2 and edit-comparison diverge (Secs. 4.1, 4.5).
Representativeness of manual evaluation sample: coverage across rare/difficult error types and datasets (Sec. 3.3).
uncertainty_flags: Small manual evaluation sample (200 edits) and 5 raters may not cover full distribution of 55 valid error-type combinations.
Discrepancy in reported percentages: per-rater 'at least 95%' claim vs. aggregated table (overall 96.3% Good+Acceptable but individual rows show some raters below 95% Good alone).
Limited detail on bootstrap testing procedure and lack of per-category significance reporting for auto vs gold reference comparisons.
Dependence on external tools (spaCy v1.6, Lancaster stemmer, Hunspell) whose errors on learner language could systematically bias classifications.
Potential dataset-specific interactions: most empirical demonstration is on CoNLL-2014 (and some FCE-test), generalization to other corpora remains partially supported.
chaining_notes: Downstream reviewers should (a) test alignment accuracy per error type and per system output (to quantify extraction errors), (b) audit classifier rules against a stratified sample of edits emphasizing rare/difficult types, and (c) reproduce bootstrap tests with explicit statistics and per-category comparisons.
Reviewers should check dependency of classification errors on POS/tagging mistakes by re-running the pipeline with alternate taggers/lemmatizers and measuring change in label quality.

For claims about reducing M2 artefacts, reviewers should identify concrete examples where M2 and the edit-comparison disagree and measure how often such disagreements change system rankings or per-category conclusions.
Where manuscript evidence is thin (bootstrap details, full rule set), reviewers should request or run additional analyses rather than take equivalence claims at face value.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that (1) linguistically-enhanced alignment plus a deterministic, rule-based, dataset-independent classifier can extract edits and assign error-type labels to unannotated GEC system outputs; (2) the resulting labels are qualitatively acceptable to human experts; (3) reprocessing gold references with the same pipeline yields system-level scores not significantly different from using original gold annotations; and (4) these auto-annotations enable detailed per-error-type analysis of CoNLL-2014 systems revealing complementary system strengths. The manuscript chains prior alignment work (Felice et al., 2016) and a set of deterministic classification rules based on automatic markup (spaCy, stemming, Hunspell) to produce annotated hypothesis and reference files, then compares system performance using these annotations. The logical flow is mostly coherent: alignment -> edit extraction -> rule-based typing -> human validation of label appropriateness -> application to CoNLL-2014 -> per-error-type analyses. However, some crucial links are under-documented or rely on assumptions: the end-to-end accuracy of extraction+classification per error type is not fully quantified (sample-based human evaluation focuses on label appropriateness conditional on auto-extracted spans and excludes boundary judgment), bootstrap testing details are sparse, and potential systematic biases from automatic markup (POS/tagging errors) and dataset idiosyncrasies are not exhaustively probed. Overall, the argument is plausible and useful, but several inferential steps need more explicit quantification or ablation to solidify claims about dataset-independence and parity with gold annotations.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Accurate edit extraction is required to compare hypotheses and references at the edit level. (Sec.2)
P2: Felice et al. (2016)’s linguistically-enhanced Damerau–Levenshtein alignment with merging rules approximates human edits (reported 80–85 F1). (Sec.2)
P3: Automatic markup (POS, lemma, stems, dependency parse, Hunspell) can be obtained for both source and target tokens. (Sec.3.1)
P4: Most human error-type labels map to linguistic properties (POS, morphological/orthographic signals), so deterministic rules on automatic markup can assign error types. (Sec.3, 3.2)
I1: Therefore, combining P2 and P3 with rule-based mapping yields automated edit extraction + dataset-independent error typing for system outputs. (C1)

E1: Human raters judged predicted categories 'Good'/'Acceptable' on a random sample (200 edits) with aggregated 96.3% Good+Acceptable and κfree 0.724 when asked to ignore boundary errors. (Sec.3.3) -> supports label appropriateness conditional on spans. (C2)
I2: Since humans accept the assigned labels on sampled edits, auto-annotation is qualitatively appropriate for per-error-type analysis. (supports C1→C4)
P5: If references are reprocessed with the same pipeline, hypothesis-reference comparisons are consistent (same extraction/classification rules applied). (Sec.4.1)

E2: Reprocessed auto references yield system-level scores not statistically different (bootstrap, 1,000 iterations, p>.05) from using gold references per Table 4. (Sec.4.1) -> supports claim that auto references are viable for evaluation. (C3)
I3: Therefore, auto-annotated hypotheses+references permit direct TP/FP/FN edit comparison and per-error-type scoring without scorer-specific boundary exploitation (e.g., M2). (C5)

E3: Applying the pipeline to CoNLL-2014 outputs produces per-team P/R/F0.5 broken down by operation tier, POS types and multi-token edits, revealing system-specific strengths (e.g., MT better at multi-token edits; classifiers better at some verb-form categories). (Sec.4, Tables 5–8) (C4)

Conclusion: The method enables dataset-independent automatic error-typing of GEC outputs that is qualitatively acceptable and enables novel per-category analyses of system behavior; however, several assumptions (alignment/per-category extraction accuracy, impact of automatic markup errors, representativeness of human sample, bootstrap test details) remain and affect the strength of equivalence claims with gold annotations.

identified_claims.claim_text: A linguistically-enhanced alignment combined with a rule-based, dataset-independent classifier can automatically extract edits and assign error types to unannotated GEC system output.
evidence: Sec.2: adoption of Felice et al. (2016) linguistically-enhanced Damerau-Levenshtein alignment and merging rules for edit extraction.
Sec.3: a deterministic rule-based classifier operating on POS, lemmas, stems, dependency parses and Hunspell non-word detection.
uncertainty_flags: The paper does not present a full, per-error-type quantitative end-to-end extraction+classification accuracy table across all categories; reliance on earlier reported alignment F1 (80–85) but not per-type breakdown.
Full rule set and edge-case rules not exhaustively listed in main text (Appendix lists valid combinations but not all classification rule logic).

identified_claims.claim_text: Human experts judged the predicted error types as 'Good' or 'Acceptable' for at least ~95% of sampled edits, indicating high qualitative appropriateness of the automatic labels.
evidence: Manual evaluation: 5 GEC researchers rated 200 randomly chosen edits (100 FCE-test, 100 CoNLL-2014) as Good/Acceptable/Bad.
Table 3: aggregated distribution — 86.3% Good, 10.0% Acceptable, 3.7% Bad; text: 'all 5 raters individually considered at least 95%... to be either Good or Acceptable.'
uncertainty_flags: Apparent inconsistency: table shows some raters with Good% below 95; the claimed 'each rater >=95% Good+Acceptable' needs explicit per-rater Good+Acceptable sums to verify.

identified_claims.claim_label: Auto references comparable to gold for scoring
identified_claims.claim_text: Reprocessing gold references with the same automatic alignment/classification pipeline yields results not statistically different from using gold annotations, validating the auto-annotation approach.
evidence: Table 4: team F0.5 scores under M2 and the paper's approach using gold vs. auto references; text reports bootstrap testing (1,000 iterations) found no significant differences (p > .05).
uncertainty_flags: Bootstrap test procedural details (resampled statistic, confidence intervals, per-category tests, multiple comparisons control) are not provided, so the claim of 'no significant difference' is under-specified.

identified_claims.claim_text: The resulting annotations enable the first detailed per-error-type evaluation of all systems in the CoNLL-2014 shared task, revealing complementary strengths/weaknesses across systems (e.g., MT better at multi-token edits; classifiers better at some verb-form categories).
evidence: Tables 5–8 present P/R/F0.5 broken down by operation tier, 24+ error types, multi-token edits and detection vs. correction.
Sec.4.5: multi-token edit performance table shows MT systems dominate multi-token correction (Table 8).
uncertainty_flags: Per-error-type conclusions depend on extraction+classification correctness per category; classifier per-category error rates are not exhaustively reported.
Some systems made no attempts at certain categories (dashes), complicating direct comparisons and generalization.

identified_claims.claim_text: The tool separates edit extraction from evaluation and reduces artefacts introduced by scorers like M2, enabling straightforward F-score comparison of edits.
evidence: Sec.4.1: describes reprocessing references so both files are compared under identical extraction/classification rules; argues M2's dynamic boundary exploitation inflates scores.
Examples and references to prior critiques (Felice & Briscoe 2015; Napoles et al. 2015) supporting scorer artefact argument.
uncertainty_flags: Separation reduces one source of scorer artefacts but introduces dependence on chosen extractor; different extractors could produce different evaluation outcomes.
Quantification of how often M2-driven boundary choices change rankings or per-category conclusions is not fully presented.

strengths.title: Clear modular pipeline tying alignment to classification
strengths.description: The paper presents a coherent pipeline: linguistically-aware alignment for edit extraction followed by a deterministic rule-based classifier using automatic linguistic markup.
evidence: Section 2 describes alignment choice (Felice et al., 2016).
Section 3 details the classifier's reliance on POS, lemma, stems, dependency parses, and Hunspell.

strengths.title: Practical utility demonstrated on real shared-task outputs
strengths.description: Authors apply the pipeline to all CoNLL-2014 system outputs and present detailed per-team, per-category metrics that reveal interpretable system behavior differences.
evidence: Tables 5–8 provide fine-grained P/R/F0.5 across teams and error types and multi-token analysis.
Section 4 reports interpretable findings (e.g., MT systems perform better on multi-token edits).

strengths.title: Transparent, interpretable rule-based classification
strengths.description: By using deterministic rules over automatic markup, the classifier yields interpretable decisions and enables precise audit of why a label was assigned.
evidence: Section 3 emphasizes determinism and ability to 'determine precisely why an edit was assigned'.
Appendix A lists valid operation-type combinations, supporting interpretability.

concerns.title: Under-quantified end-to-end extraction+classification accuracy per error type
concerns.description: The paper lacks a comprehensive, per-error-type quantitative evaluation of the combined alignment+classification pipeline; claimed equivalence to gold is shown at aggregate scores but not exhaustively per category or per system.
evidence: Shared analysis notes reliance on Felice et al. (2016) alignment F1 for extraction but no per-category extraction error rates in this manuscript.
Bootstrap test summary in Sec.4.1 lacks per-category results and test details.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a stratified evaluation: (a) measure alignment/extraction boundary accuracy per error type and per edit size; (b) report end-to-end precision/recall/F1 for classification per error category using a larger stratified manual gold sample (including rare types); (c) include confusion matrices showing common misclassifications.

concerns.title: Manual evaluation sample and framing limit representativeness
concerns.description: Classifier evaluation is based on 200 randomly sampled edits rated by 5 experts who were instructed to ignore boundary quality; this validates label appropriateness conditional on spans but does not validate end-to-end labels including boundaries or coverage across 55 possible type combinations.
evidence: Sec.3.3 describes 200 edits (100 FCE + 100 CoNLL) and Table 3 shows per-rater Good/Acceptable/Bad distributions.
Shared analysis points out possible under-representation of rare/difficult types.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Expand manual evaluation to a larger, stratified sample across datasets and error types (especially low-frequency and multi-token edits), and include a separate evaluation where raters judge end-to-end correctness (including boundaries).

concerns.title: Dependence on automatic markup not fully stress-tested
concerns.description: Classifier correctness depends on automatic POS/lemma/parse/stem quality, which is known to degrade on learner language; the paper acknowledges POS-tagging causes many 'Bad' cases but lacks systematic ablation showing sensitivity to markup errors.
evidence: Sec.3.1 lists spaCy v1.6, Lancaster stemmer and Hunspell; Sec.3.3 states 'Bad' ratings usually traced to POS tagger mistakes.
Shared analysis recommends re-running with alternate taggers to measure impact.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report an ablation where the classification is rerun with alternative taggers/lemmatizers/parsers (or gold tags where available) on a subset, and quantify changes in label quality per category.

concerns.title: Bootstrap significance reporting under-specified
concerns.description: The claim of no statistical difference between auto and gold references rests on a bootstrap test (1,000 iterations, p>.05) but the exact tested statistic, handling of multiple comparisons, and per-category results are not reported.
evidence: Sec.4.1 describes the bootstrap validation but provides no test statistic or per-category numbers; Table 4 only shows aggregate team scores.
Shared analysis flags need for explicit bootstrap details.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include precise bootstrap procedure details (resampled unit, statistic computed, CI reporting), report per-team and per-category confidence intervals and p-values, and correct for multiple comparisons where relevant.

concerns.title: Dataset-independence claim needs broader empirical support
concerns.description: The classifier is designed to be dataset-independent but empirical demonstration is primarily on CoNLL-2014 (plus some FCE-test sampling); generalization to other learner corpora or tokenization/annotation conventions is asserted but not exhaustively shown.
evidence: Paper applies pipeline to CoNLL-2014 and samples FCE-test for manual rating but does not show cross-corpus per-category metrics beyond those.
Shared analysis notes potential dataset-specific interactions (tokenization, error distribution).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Apply the pipeline to at least one additional distinct learner corpus (with different conventions) and report per-category outcomes or show classifier stability under differing tokenization/annotation conventions.

comparable_works.relevance: Source of the linguistically-enhanced alignment method used and reported extraction F1 baseline (80-85).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Directly adopted alignment approach; paper builds on Felice et al. for extraction but differs by adding deterministic dataset-independent error typing and applying it to system outputs.
comparable_works.source_trace: Sec.2 references and shared analysis

comparable_works.relevance: Early automatic edit extraction and error-type classification (Levenshtein + classifier); motivates rule-based, dataset-agnostic approach.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Swanson/Yamangil used ML classifiers trained on data; current paper contrasts with a rule-based, dataset-independent classifier.
comparable_works.source_trace: Sec.2 and 3 references

comparable_works.relevance: Work on predicting merge/split decisions for edits; contextual precedent for merging rules.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Provides alternative ML approach to merging; the present paper uses hand-crafted merging rules within a linguistically-weighted alignment.
comparable_works.source_trace: Sec.2 references

comparable_works.citation_label: M2 scorer (Dahlmeier & Ng, 2012) and critiques (Felice & Briscoe 2015; Napoles et al. 2015)
comparable_works.relevance: Standard GEC evaluation scorer whose dynamic boundaries the paper critiques; used as baseline comparison in Sec.4.1.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Paper contrasts its fixed-span comparison approach against M2's dynamic boundary matching and provides examples of M2's inflation of scores.
comparable_works.source_trace: Sec.4.1 discussion and Table 4

uncertainty_flags: Aggregate bootstrap non-significance (p>.05) may conceal per-category or per-system differences—bootstrap procedure is underspecified.
Manual rating sample is small and instructed to ignore boundary quality; thus label appropriateness assessed conditionally on extracted spans, not end-to-end pipeline correctness.
Automatic markup (POS/lemmatization/parsing) errors on learner text may systematically bias certain error-type assignments (e.g., NOUN vs VERB), and sensitivity to different taggers is untested.
Extraction errors (merge/split/boundary mistakes) may differentially affect systems that produce different edit styles, biasing comparative per-type scores.
Dataset-independence asserted but empirical coverage beyond CoNLL-2014 and an FCE sample is limited.
alternative_interpretations: High human acceptability of labels (Good/Acceptable) primarily reflects accurate category heuristics given correct spans; the end-to-end pipeline may still misassign many edits due to boundary errors, which raters were asked to ignore.

Aggregate equivalence between auto and gold references may hold for overall F0.5 but hide systematic per-category shifts: some categories may be consistently under/over-represented after auto-processing.

Apparent system strengths (e.g., MT better at multi-token edits) could partly reflect extractor favorability toward contiguous multi-token changes that resemble MT outputs, rather than inherent system superiority.
transparency_notes: Appendix A lists valid operation-code combinations (55 total) but full deterministic rule logic for mapping markup patterns to categories is not exhaustively included in the main text; releasing the full rule set and code (which authors state they will) is necessary for reproducibility.
Bootstrap testing procedure should be fully specified (resampling unit, statistic, per-comparison reporting) to allow reproduction.
The paper documents the external tools used (spaCy v1.6, Lancaster stemmer, Hunspell) which enables reproduction but also requires specifying model versions and tagger configuration details.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: Although rule-based error typing has precursors, the combination of linguistically-enhanced extraction plus a deterministic, dataset-independent type taxonomy applied to mass system outputs is a novel, practically useful contribution. Novelty does not guarantee end-to-end validity: the pipeline's outputs require per-category verification and sensitivity analyses to tagging/alignment choices.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If alignment quality (Felice et al. method) maintains high boundary accuracy across all key error types (including multi-token edits), then the rule-based classifier will achieve high end-to-end per-category accuracy.

If automatic linguistic markup (POS/lemmas/parses) is robust on learner data (or replaced with more accurate models / gold annotations) then classification errors attributable to tagger mistakes will drop substantially.

If expanded manual evaluation stratified by error type confirms high per-category label correctness (not just conditional on spans), then auto-annotation will be validated for broad use in evaluations and corpora standardization.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The pipeline fills a practical gap: unannotated system outputs can be analyzed per-error-type, enabling analyses previously impossible at scale.
evidence: Application to CoNLL-2014 and resulting per-team per-type tables (Tables 5–8).
uncertainty_flags: Utility depends on end-to-end reliability per category, which needs more quantification.

novelty_lenses.rationale: While rule-based typing and linguistically-informed alignment exist separately in prior work, their composition into a deterministic, dataset-agnostic annotation-and-evaluation pipeline applied to system outputs is a novel methodology with operational benefits.
evidence: Paper explicitly contrasts ML-based classifiers' dataset bias and proposes deterministic rules for dataset-independence (Sec.3).
uncertainty_flags: Degree of novelty conditioned on completeness of the rule set and breadth of empirical validation across corpora.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Key validity risks stem from alignment boundary errors, dependence on automatic markup, and limited manual validation; these could undermine per-category claims even if aggregate scores look similar.
evidence: Acknowledged POS-tagging mistakes linked to 'Bad' ratings; absence of per-category extraction accuracy.
uncertainty_flags: Extent to which these risks affect different error types or system comparisons is not quantified in the manuscript.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately to highly confident in the paper's core engineering claim (pipeline can produce plausible annotations and enable analyses) given the demonstrated application to CoNLL-2014 and human-rating evidence; however, confidence is reduced by under-specified statistical testing, limited stratified manual validation, and dependence on automatic markup—hence the interval reflects this uncertainty.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a deterministic pipeline to auto-annotate GEC system outputs with explicit edit spans and dataset-independent error types: (1) use a linguistically-enhanced Damerau-Levenshtein alignment with merging rules (Felice et al. 2016) to extract token-level edit spans; (2) apply a rule-based classifier relying only on automatic markup (spaCy POS/lemma/deps, Lancaster stemmer, Hunspell) to assign labels from a 25+ type taxonomy, optionally prefixed by operation tier (Missing/Replacement/Unnecessary). The authors validate label appropriateness via a 200-edit manual rating by 5 expert raters (Good/Acceptable/Bad, κfree=0.724) and compare system-level scores computed using auto-annotated references against original gold references (bootstrap testing, 1,000 iterations, p>.05). They then auto-annotate all CoNLL-2014 system outputs and present per-type P/R/F0.5 analyses, multi-token analysis, and detection-vs-correction curves, arguing the pipeline enables more transparent per-error-type evaluation and avoids scorer boundary artefacts (e.g., M2’s dynamic merging). The claimed benefits rest on (a) adequate alignment/span extraction quality, (b) sufficiently accurate automatic linguistic markup, (c) representativeness of the manual sample for classifier validation, and (d) robustness of bootstrap non-significance conclusions. Key evidence presented: description of the pipeline, Table 3 (manual ratings), Table 4 (gold vs auto references comparison), detailed per-team per-type tables (Tables 5–8), and κfree agreement.
logical_argument_graph: If we can extract edit spans from original/corrected sentence pairs with sufficient fidelity (using linguistically-enhanced alignment), then we can produce deterministic, fixed spans for hypotheses and references.
If edits are represented with consistent spans and automatic linguistic markup, then a rule-based classifier (operating only on this markup) can assign interpretable, dataset-independent error types.
If human experts rate the assigned types as appropriate at high rates, then the classifier is qualitatively adequate for analysis purposes.

If reprocessing gold references with the same extraction/classification yields system scores not significantly different from using original gold annotations, then auto-annotated references are acceptable for system-level comparisons.
Therefore, auto-annotating all system outputs enables per-error-type P/R/F0.5 analyses and reveals complementary system strengths/weaknesses while avoiding scorer boundary artefacts like those in M2.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a pragmatic pipeline to auto-annotate Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) system outputs with linguistically-informed edit spans and dataset-independent error types. The pipeline reuses a linguistically-enhanced Damerau–Levenshtein alignment (Felice et al., 2016) to extract edit spans and applies a deterministic rule-based classifier that relies on automatically-obtained token properties (coarse POS, lemmas, stems, dependency info, Hunspell) to assign one of 55 possible error-type codes (operation tier × POS / morphology). The authors validate label appropriateness with a 200-edit human rating (5 expert raters) and argue that reprocessing gold references with the same pipeline produces system scores statistically indistinguishable from using original gold annotations (bootstrap test). They then present a detailed per-error-type analysis of all CoNLL-2014 systems, illustrating complementary strengths across system architectures (MT, classifiers, LM, rules). The manuscript's reasoning chain is: alignment -> deterministic extraction rules -> auto-markup -> rule-based classification -> annotate both hypotheses and references identically -> direct edit span matching for evaluation -> human and bootstrap-based validation -> per-error-type system analyses. The contribution is best understood as a meaningful incremental advance: it combines prior alignment work with a comprehensively-designed, deterministic, dataset-agnostic error-type taxonomy and tooling to enable analyses that were previously impractical. Key risks to the claimed impact are dependence on alignment/span quality, sensitivity to automatic linguistic annotation (POS/tagging) on learner data, limited manual validation coverage (200 edits), and somewhat underspecified statistical testing and rule transparency in the main text.
logical_argument_graph: Problem: system outputs in shared tasks are unannotated so per-error-type evaluation is infeasible
Premise: Existing linguistically-enhanced alignments can approximate human edits (~80-85 F1)
Step 1: Apply Felice et al. (2016) enhanced Damerau–Levenshtein alignment + merging rules to extract edit spans
Step 2: Auto-mark tokens (spaCy POS/lemmas, Lancaster stemmer, Hunspell, UD mapping) to obtain deterministic features
Step 3: Apply rule-based classifier (dataset-independent, deterministic) to assign error-type codes (55 variants)
Step 4: Reprocess references with same pipeline so hypotheses & references share format; compare identical span+correction pairs -> TP/FP/FN
Validation A: Manual rating (200 edits × 5 expert raters) to assess label appropriateness
Validation B: Bootstrap testing comparing auto vs gold references for system-level scores (no significant difference reported)
Result: Enables first broad per-error-type scoring of CoNLL-2014 systems and identifies complementary strengths across system classes
Conclusion: Deterministic, dataset-independent annotation pipeline facilitates standardized per-error-type evaluation and reduces scorer artefacts (e.g., M2 dynamic boundary exploitation)

strengths.title: Enables analyses previously infeasible
strengths.description: Annotating hypotheses and references identically makes per-error-type P/R/F0.5 comparisons straightforward, allowing detailed system-level and operation-tier insights across CoNLL-2014 teams.

strengths.description: The taxonomy permits independent evaluation at multiple granularities (Missing/Replacement/Unnecessary × POS/morph classes), useful for focused diagnostics and combination with other analyses.

concerns.title: Dependence on alignment/span extraction quality
concerns.description: The pipeline's correctness fundamentally depends on the alignment algorithm's ability to recover human-like edit spans; alignment boundary errors (splits/merges) can cause downstream misclassification and distort per-type P/R/F0.5 comparisons.
evidence: Sec. 2 relies on Felice et al. (2016) alignment claiming 80–85 F1 approximating human edits; shared analysis notes this assumption (A1).
Authors acknowledge that a hypothetical edit [have eating → has eaten] vs two separate edits illustrates boundary mismatch impact (Sec. 4.1).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a stratified analysis of alignment accuracy per error category (TP/FP/FN for span extraction) and measure how often alignment-induced merges/splits change the assigned error type; include confusion matrices or per-type span-F1 so readers can judge extraction error rates.

concerns.title: Limited manual validation sample and coverage
concerns.description: The human evaluation used 200 edits and 5 raters; this sample may underrepresent rare or difficult error types and does not measure end-to-end correctness (raters were instructed to ignore boundary issues), so claims of '95% Good+Acceptable' may overstate general classifier reliability.
evidence: Sec. 3.3: 200 randomly chosen edits (100 FCE, 100 CoNLL-2014) rated by 5 experts; shared analysis flags representativeness risk (A3).
Raters told to ignore boundary quality, thus conditional assessment only.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Expand manual evaluation with stratified sampling across all error categories (oversample rare/difficult types), increase sample size, and run a complementary end-to-end annotation check where raters judge both span and label together to capture alignment-induced mislabels.

concerns.title: Underspecified statistical testing for auto vs gold references
concerns.description: The bootstrap significance claim (1,000 iterations, p > .05) lacks details (resampling unit, statistic tested, per-category testing, multiple comparisons), making it hard to evaluate the strength of the equivalence claim between auto and gold references.
evidence: Sec. 4.1 states bootstrap testing used but gives limited methodological detail; shared analysis lists A7 as an identified assumption.
Authors conclude 'no statistically significant difference' but do not present per-category results or confidence intervals.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report exact test statistics: resampling unit (sentence/team), test statistic distribution, confidence intervals, and per-category p-values with multiple-comparison control; provide effect sizes to show practical equivalence, not just non-significance.

concerns.title: Sensitivity to automatic linguistic markup accuracy on learner data
concerns.description: The rule-based classifier relies on spaCy POS/lemmas and other automatic annotations which can perform poorly on learner text, causing systematic misclassification (authors note some 'Bad' ratings traced to POS errors).
evidence: Sec. 3.1 lists spaCy v1.6, Lancaster stemmer, Hunspell as prerequisites; Sec. 3.3 reports that 'Bad' ratings usually trace back to POS tagger mistakes.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Quantify classifier sensitivity to tagging errors: rerun a sample with alternative taggers/lemmatizers or use oracle tags on a held-out set to estimate the upper bound; include a breakdown of 'Bad' cases showing which automatic feature failed and how rule logic could be made robust.

concerns.title: Generalisability beyond evaluated corpora
concerns.description: Although the classifier is designed to be dataset-independent, empirical demonstration focuses on CoNLL-2014 (and some FCE); differences in tokenization, annotation conventions, and learner error distributions could affect comparability across other corpora.
evidence: Paper emphasizes dataset-agnostic design (Sec. 3) but empirical application and analysis are concentrated on CoNLL-2014; shared analysis notes limited evidence for robustness across corpora (A6).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Demonstrate portability by applying the pipeline to at least one other publicly available corpus (beyond the 100 FCE edits sampled), report per-category changes, and document any dataset-specific pre-processing steps required.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a deterministic, dataset-independent pipeline to auto-annotate Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) system outputs with explicit edit spans and linguistically-informed error types. The pipeline (1) extracts edits using a linguistically-enhanced Damerau–Levenshtein alignment with merging rules (Felice et al. style) and (2) classifies edits using a rule-based classifier that relies on automatic markup (POS, lemma, stems, dependency parses, Hunspell) into a 25-type taxonomy with operation-tier prefixes (M:/R:/U:). The authors validate classifier label appropriateness via a small manual rating (200 edits × 5 expert raters), report >95% Good+Acceptable per rater (table shows overall 96.3%), and show that reprocessing gold references with the same pipeline yields team-level scores not statistically different from originals (bootstrap, 1,000 iterations, p>.05). They then auto-annotate all CoNLL-2014 system outputs and present comprehensive per-error-type P/R/F0.5 analyses, multi-token edit analyses, and detection-vs-correction comparisons. The central argumentative chain is: dataset-independent deterministic rules + linguistically-informed alignment produce usable annotations → humans judge categories largely appropriate → auto-annotated references are interchangeable with gold for system-level scoring → therefore the pipeline enables reliable per-error-type evaluation and reveals complementary strengths among systems. The paper emphasizes reproducibility and separating extraction from scoring to avoid scorer artefacts (e.g., M2 dynamic boundary exploitation).
logical_argument_graph: P1: Current GEC system outputs are unannotated; thus per-error-type evaluation across systems is infeasible.
P2: Linguistically-enhanced alignment (Felice-like) can approximate human edit spans (reported 80-85 F1 in prior work).
P3: A rule-based classifier using only automatic markup yields dataset-independent labels and is transparent/deterministic.
P4: Manual ratings (200 edits × 5 raters) indicate high appropriateness (Good+Acceptable ≈ 96.3%).
P5: Reprocessing gold references with the pipeline yields no significant difference in team-level scores (bootstrap p>.05).
C1: Therefore, the pipeline can auto-annotate unannotated GEC outputs with linguistically-informed spans and dataset-independent error types.
C2: Therefore, auto-annotated references support meaningful per-error-type evaluation (precision/recall/F0.5) and comparisons across systems.
C3: Separating extraction from scoring reduces scorer artefacts (e.g., M2’s merging behavior) and increases transparency/reproducibility.
Edge notes: Several assumptions (alignment reliability, markup accuracy, manual sample representativeness) underpin P2–P5 and thus condition confidence in C1–C3.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a deterministic, dataset-independent pipeline that (1) extracts edit spans using a linguistically-enhanced Damerau-Levenshtein alignment (Felice et al., 2016 + merging rules) and (2) classifies edits into a 25-type taxonomy (expandable to 55 codes with operation prefixes) via rule-based decisions on automatic linguistic markup (spaCy POS/lemmas, Lancaster stemmer, Hunspell, dependency info). The authors validate the classifier by asking 5 expert GEC researchers to rate 200 randomly sampled auto-extracted edits (100 FCE, 100 CoNLL-2014) as Good/Acceptable/Bad, reporting aggregated Good+Acceptable ≈ 96.3% and κfree=0.724. They also reprocess gold references with the same pipeline and report no statistically significant differences in team-level F0.5 scores (bootstrap, 1,000 iterations, p>.05). Applying the pipeline to all CoNLL-2014 system outputs yields detailed per-error-type precision/recall/F0.5 tables and analyses (operation tier, multi-token edits, detection vs. correction). The logical chain is: alignment -> edit extraction -> rule-based typing (using automatic markup) -> manual rating of label appropriateness conditional on extracted spans -> reprocessing references with same pipeline -> per-error-type system analysis. Evidence in the manuscript supports most intermediate claims, but key inferential steps (end-to-end extraction+classification accuracy per error type; detailed bootstrap/statistical reporting; sensitivity to automatic markup and alignment errors) are under-documented. I separate claims supported by presented evidence from those that are only partially supported or potentially overstated below, and flag uncertainties and recommended analyses to solidify conclusions.
logical_argument_graph: Prior alignment method (Felice et al., 2016) + merging rules => linguistically-enhanced alignment suitable for extracting edit spans (Sec.2).
Extracted spans + automatic markup (spaCy POS/lemmas, Lancaster stemmer, Hunspell, dependency info) => rule-based classifier assigns dataset-independent error-type codes (Sec.3, Table 2, Appendix A).
Manual rating of 200 auto-extracted edits by 5 experts => high label appropriateness (Good/Acceptable ≈96.3%) and acceptable inter-rater agreement κfree=0.724 (Sec.3.3, Table 3).
Reprocessing gold references through same pipeline and comparing team F0.5 scores with bootstrap => no significant differences (Sec.4.1, Table 4).
Annotating hypotheses + references identically => direct span+correction matching for TP/FP/FN and per-error-type P/R/F0.5 analyses across CoNLL-2014 systems (Sec.4, Tables 5–8).
Observed per-error-type patterns (e.g., MT better at multi-token; classifiers better on some verb forms) => actionable insights about complementary strengths (Sec.4.2–4.6).

strengths.title: Practical demonstration at scale
strengths.description: Applied the tool to all CoNLL-2014 system outputs and produced comprehensive per-error-type P/R/F0.5 analyses, multi-token analyses, and detection-vs-correction comparisons.

concerns.description: Only 200 edits (100 per dataset split) were rated by 5 experts; this small sample likely under-represents rare/complex categories and multi-token edits, limiting claims about classifier performance across all 55 possible codes.

alternative_interpretations: High Good+Acceptable ratings mostly show that, when the extractor provides a coherent span, the rule-based classifier maps that span to a reasonable category — but this does not guarantee that the pipeline produces correct span+label pairs at the same rate; end-to-end errors may be larger.

Aggregate team-level equivalence between auto and gold references could arise because reprocessing alters references in ways that cancel out across many edits, hiding per-category misalignments that would matter for fine-grained error-type analyses.

Observed system strengths (e.g., MT better at multi-token edits) might partly reflect the extractor’s sensitivity to certain edit styles — i.e., systems that produce contiguous multi-token edits are easier for this extractor to capture, inflating their apparent advantage.

The dataset-independence claim is plausible as a design goal, but performance may degrade on corpora with different tokenization/annotation habits or on learner varieties that break POS taggers; thus 'dataset-independent' should be taken as 'dataset-agnostic rule design' rather than empirically proven transferability.
transparency_notes: The manuscript provides taxonomy and valid code combinations (Appendix A) which aids reproducibility; however, full classifier rule list, rule ordering/priority, and exact merging thresholds are not exhaustively specified in the main text—these should be published alongside the tool.

The authors note tool release; sharing code, configuration (spaCy model/version), and processed annotated CoNLL-2014 files will materially improve auditing and reuse.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The pipeline's combination of linguistically-enhanced alignment with a dataset-independent deterministic rule-based error-typing framework, applied at scale to annotate hypotheses and references alike, appears uncommon in the corpus and signals practical innovation. However, novelty does not imply correctness: empirical validity depends on end-to-end extraction+classification fidelity, sensitivity to automatic markup, and reproducibility of statistical claims.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the alignment method truly achieves high boundary accuracy across error types (e.g., ≥80 F1 per Felice et al.), then downstream deterministic rules will receive coherent spans and per-type classification will be reliable.
If modern POS/lemma/tagging tools (or ensemble taggers) are used and perform robustly on learner data, classifier rules using POS/lemma features will correctly disambiguate many categories.

If reprocessing gold references preserves the semantic equivalence of edits and any introduced differences are random (not systematic by category or system), then aggregate team-level scoring equivalence will hold and per-type comparisons will be meaningful.
If the authors publish full rules and configuration and practitioners reproduce key tables on held-out corpora, the approach will be validated as both reproducible and generally applicable.

uncertainty_flags: Novelty is clear as an applied product, but empirical validation (end-to-end per-type reliability) needs strengthening to realize full impact.

uncertainty_flags: This disruptive potential depends on robust, reproducible equivalence to gold at per-category level and community acceptance; current evidence is promising but not yet conclusive.

confidence_interval.rationale: I have medium-high confidence in the manuscript's core engineering contribution (pipeline design, taxonomy, and large-scale application) and moderate confidence in the qualitative classifier appropriateness claim (based on small manual sample). consensus_findings: The manuscript presents a coherent, modular pipeline that combines a linguistically-enhanced alignment (Felice-style) with a deterministic, rule-based, dataset-agnostic error-type classifier and applies it to annotate both hypotheses and references for large-scale per-error-type evaluation.

Applying the pipeline to CoNLL-2014 system outputs produced novel, interpretable per-error-type P/R/F0.5 analyses and diagnostic breakdowns (operation tiers, multi-token edits, detection vs. correction) that are practically useful for system comparison.

A manual evaluation (200 auto-extracted edits rated by 5 expert GEC annotators) indicates that, conditional on the extracted spans, the assigned categories are judged 'Good' or 'Acceptable' at high rates (authors report aggregated Good+Acceptable ≈ 96.3% and per-rater Good+Acceptable ≥ 95%).

Reprocessing gold references with the same pipeline and comparing team-level F0.5 scores yields no statistically significant difference at the aggregate team level under the reported bootstrap test (1,000 iterations; p > .05), suggesting auto-annotated references can approximate aggregate scoring under some conditions.

The approach increases interpretability and reproducibility by making classification deterministic and by separating extraction from evaluation, thereby surfacing evaluation artefacts that scorers like M2 can introduce via dynamic boundary handling.
disagreements: Whether aggregate non-significance (auto vs gold references) suffices to claim equivalence for fine-grained per-error-type evaluation: some reviewers accept aggregate bootstrap results as supportive, others find bootstrap details and per-category tests insufficient to support that claim.

Degree to which the 200-edit manual sample supports broad classifier reliability: some reviewers consider the conditional Good+Acceptable rates persuasive for common categories, while others judge the sample too small and not stratified across the full taxonomy to generalize.

Severity of dependence on automatic markup (POS/lemma/parse/stemming/Hunspell): some reviewers view this as an engineering dependency explaining most 'Bad' cases, others view it as a major validity risk that requires ablation with alternate taggers or oracle tags.

Extent of novelty and impact: some reviewers frame the contribution as a meaningful, enabling incremental tool (first large-scale per-type CoNLL-2014 analysis), while others emphasize that components are recombinations of prior work and that the practical impact depends on stronger per-type and robustness validation.
uncertainty_hotspots: End-to-end extraction+classification accuracy per error type is under-specified: the manuscript reports conditional label appropriateness but not combined span+label agreement stratified by category (no per-type extraction precision/recall/F1 or combined metrics).

Bootstrap testing details are insufficiently documented: the tested statistic(s), resampling unit (sentence vs. team), confidence intervals, per-team/per-category p-values, and multiple-comparison handling are not reported, leaving uncertainty about the robustness of the aggregate non-significance claim and about localized differences.

Manual evaluation representativeness: 200 randomly sampled edits likely under-represents low-frequency and multi-token error types; raters were instructed to ignore boundary quality, so ratings speak to label appropriateness conditioned on spans rather than end-to-end correctness.

Sensitivity to automatic linguistic markup and external tools (spaCy v1.6, Lancaster stemmer, Hunspell): systematic POS/lemma/parse errors on learner data could induce category-specific misclassifications; reviewers identified a lack of ablation/sensitivity experiments using alternative tools or oracle tags.

Potential extractor-system interaction bias: merging/splitting rules and alignment decisions may interact with different systems' editing styles (e.g., MT producing contiguous multi-token edits), possibly producing system-dependent artefacts that could confound per-type comparisons.
model_diversity_effects: Methodology-focused reviewers emphasize reproducibility and stress-tested validity: they request missing procedural details (bootstrap code, rule ordering, merging thresholds), ablations, and per-category metrics, treating conditional manual ratings as insufficient.

Structure/logic-focused reviewers accept the pipeline's internal coherence but flag under-documented inferential steps (alignment→classification chaining) and request stratified error analyses to close the chain.

Novelty assessors split between viewing the work as practically enabling (deterministic, dataset-agnostic tooling applied at scale) and viewing it as an incremental recombination whose broader impact depends on robustness checks; this produces mixed recommendations about readiness for general adoption.

Claim verifiers concentrate on evidence-claim alignment and urge precise disambiguation of reported statistics (e.g., per-rater Good vs Good+Acceptable) and clear labeling of which validations are conditional on extracted spans versus end-to-end pipeline performance.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Center editorial decisions on whether the manuscript should be treated as an enabling tool that needs targeted additional validation or as a fully validated methodology ready for broad claims. If revisions are requested, require authors to: (a) provide stratified, per-error-type end-to-end extraction+classification metrics separating span and label errors; (b) fully specify and publish bootstrap testing code and report per-team and per-category confidence intervals and p-values or equivalence-test style results; (c) run ablations with at least one alternative POS/lemma/tagging pipeline (and, where possible, an oracle-tag subset) to quantify sensitivity; (d) quantify extractor behavior per system (split/merge/boundary rates) and show whether per-type conclusions hold under sensitivity analyses; and (e) release the full deterministic rule set, merging heuristics, and processed annotated files and scripts to reproduce key tables and plots. Keep the editor role central: ask authors to temper broad dataset-independence/equivalence claims until cross-corpus validation and per-category statistical reporting are provided or explicitly caveated.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen empirical claims and reproducibility, provide the following before wider dissemination: (1) A stratified manual audit that samples edits by error type (including rare and multi-token types) and has annotators judge both span boundaries and label correctness so you can report per-type extraction precision/recall/F1 and combined span+label agreement with confusion matrices. (2) Bootstrap & statistical transparency: publish the exact bootstrap procedure (resampling unit, test statistic), provide confidence intervals, per-team and per-category p-values or equivalence-test results, and control for multiple comparisons or report effect sizes. (3) Robustness ablations: rerun the classifier with at least one alternative POS/lemma/tagging pipeline and, where feasible, an oracle-tagged subset to quantify how many 'Bad' cases stem from markup errors and which categories are most sensitive. (4) Extractor sensitivity: measure per-system merge/split/boundary error rates and run sensitivity experiments (e.g., alternative merging thresholds or an alternate extractor) to assess whether per-type conclusions are extractor-dependent. (5) Full release and documentation: publish the complete rule set (decision order, tie-breaking, edge-case rules), merging parameters, exact external-tool versions/configs, processed annotated CoNLL-2014 files, and scripts to reproduce tables/plots. (6) Clarify wording in the manuscript to disambiguate per-rater vs aggregate statistics and explicitly mark which validations are conditional on extracted spans versus end-to-end performance.
transparency_report: The manuscript documents the high-level pipeline, taxonomy, and which external tools were used (spaCy v1.6, Lancaster stemmer, Hunspell) and includes Appendix A enumerating valid operation-type combinations, which aids reproducibility.

Missing: the full deterministic rule set (complete decision logic, rule ordering, tie-breaking, and edge-case handling) is not exhaustively listed in the main text or appendix; authors should release this alongside code.

Missing: precise alignment/merging parameterization and exact implementation of merging heuristics (thresholds, cost schemes) are not fully specified; these determine span extraction behavior and should be published.

Missing: bootstrap testing methodology is underspecified (resampling unit, statistic, CI computation, per-category reporting, multiple-comparison handling); authors should provide code and seeds to reproduce tests.

Missing: processed auto-annotated reference and hypothesis files used to produce the per-type analyses and scripts to recreate tables/plots have not been made available; releasing these is necessary for independent auditing.
Missing: explicit versioning and configuration details for external tools (exact spaCy model file, Hunspell dictionary, tokenizer settings, random seeds) should be listed in a reproducibility README.
epistemic_limits: Conditional validation: the human evaluation demonstrates label appropriateness conditional on auto-extracted spans, but it does not quantify end-to-end span+label correctness across the full taxonomy. Therefore, the provided ratings cannot alone establish full pipeline accuracy.

Aggregate vs local inference: the reported non-significant aggregate team-level differences (bootstrap p>.05) do not guarantee per-category or per-system equivalence; aggregate non-significance can mask meaningful localized discrepancies important for per-error-type evaluation.

Dependence on external modules: classifier correctness depends on the accuracy of automatic POS/lemma/parse/stem/non-word detection on learner text. Without robustness checks across taggers or oracle baselines, it is unclear how much misclassification is due to classifier logic versus upstream tool errors.

Extractor-mediated effects: alignment and merging decisions can systematically change how edits are split/merged, producing evaluation artifacts that may correlate with certain system styles; without per-system extraction sensitivity analyses, attribution of system strengths/weaknesses remains uncertain.

Generalisability boundary: claims of dataset-independence are design-driven but empirically demonstrated mainly on CoNLL-2014 (with a small FCE sample). Absent broader cross-corpus validation, generalizability to different annotation/tokenization conventions or learner varieties remains provisional.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript describes a deterministic, linguistically-informed pipeline that (1) extracts edit spans from sentence pairs using a linguistically-enhanced Damerau–Levenshtein alignment with merging rules and (2) assigns dataset-independent error-type labels via a rule-based classifier that uses automatic POS/lemma/stem/parse and non-word detection. The authors apply the pipeline to annotate both hypotheses and gold references, validate label appropriateness on a 200-edit manual sample (5 expert raters), compare auto-reprocessed references to original golds via bootstrap testing at team-level, and produce the first large-scale per-error-type analyses of CoNLL-2014 system outputs. Reviewers agree the pipeline is coherent, practically useful, and increases transparency for per-type analyses; they also agree important validation and reporting gaps remain (end-to-end per-type accuracy, bootstrap procedural detail, sensitivity to automatic markup, and extractor-system interaction).
strengths: Clear, modular pipeline that separates edit extraction, deterministic classification, and evaluation, enabling focused audits and reuse of components.

Practical demonstration at scale: the pipeline is applied to all CoNLL-2014 system outputs producing interpretable per-error-type P/R/F0.5 breakdowns, multi-token analyses, and detection-vs-correction diagnostics.
Deterministic, rule-based classifier using only automatic markup increases interpretability and supports dataset-agnostic deployment (by design) and reproducibility if rules/code are released.

Manual expert ratings show high conditional label appropriateness (authors report aggregated Good+Acceptable ≈ 96.3% and per-rater Good+Acceptable ≥ 95%), supporting practical usefulness of the label mapping when spans are reasonable.
limitations: End-to-end extraction+classification accuracy per error type is under-characterized: manual validation intentionally asked raters to ignore boundary quality, so reported Good/Acceptable rates measure label appropriateness conditional on extracted spans rather than combined span+label correctness — the manuscript lacks stratified per-type span-F1 and combined span+label agreement.

Statistical testing details are underspecified: the reported bootstrap comparison (1,000 iterations; p > .05) between auto-reprocessed and gold references omits the exact tested statistic, resampling unit, confidence intervals, per-team/per-category results, and multiple-comparison handling, leaving the equivalence claim for fine-grained analyses unsubstantiated.

Dependence on automatic linguistic markup (spaCy v1.6, Lancaster stemmer, Hunspell) is not stress-tested: the paper notes many 'Bad' cases trace to POS-tagging errors but provides no ablation with alternative taggers or oracle tags to quantify sensitivity and which categories are most affected.

Potential extractor-system interaction bias is not quantified: merging/splitting/ boundary heuristics may interact with different systems' editing styles (e.g., MT multi-token edits), so per-type differences across systems may partly reflect extractor behavior rather than intrinsic system strengths.
open_questions: Please provide stratified end-to-end evaluation: what are per-error-type extraction precision/recall/F1 and combined span+label agreement rates (with confusion matrices) over a larger, stratified manual sample that includes rare and multi-token types?

Please detail the bootstrap procedure used for the gold vs auto-reference comparison: what statistic was tested, what was the resampling unit (sentence, edit, document, or team), what confidence intervals and p-values per team and per error-type were obtained, and how were multiple comparisons handled?

How sensitive are classification outcomes to the upstream tagger/lemmatizer/parser? Please report ablation results rerunning the pipeline with at least one alternative tagging pipeline (or an oracle-tag subset) and quantify how many 'Bad' cases and which categories change.

Can you quantify extractor-induced biases per system? Provide per-system rates of split/merge/boundary mismatches relative to a human-aligned gold sample and show whether the main per-type conclusions (e.g., MT advantage on multi-token edits) persist under alternative merging thresholds or another extractor.
consensus_snapshot: The pipeline is coherent and practically useful: a linguistically-enhanced alignment plus deterministic rule-based classifier can generate interpretable per-error-type annotations for unannotated system outputs.
Applying the pipeline to CoNLL-2014 produced novel and actionable per-error-type analyses that were previously infeasible at scale.
Manual ratings by expert annotators indicate high conditional label appropriateness when judged on assigned spans.

Key methodological and reporting gaps remain that limit confidence in fine-grained or generalization claims: end-to-end per-type accuracy, bootstrap procedural transparency, robustness to automatic markup, and system-dependent extractor effects.
disagreement_snapshot: Some reviewers regard the aggregate bootstrap non-significance as suggestive that auto-annotated references approximate gold sufficiently for system-level scoring; others find the bootstrap underspecification and lack of per-category tests prevent strong empirical support for equivalence, especially for per-type evaluation.

Reviewers differ on whether the 200-edit manual sample (5 raters) is adequate: some view the conditional Good+Acceptable rates as meaningful support for common categories, while others consider the sample too small and unstratified to generalize across 25+/55 code combinations and multi-token edits.

Opinions diverge on novelty framing: several reviewers call this a useful, meaningful incremental engineering contribution (integration + tooling), while a minority emphasize that components are recombinations of prior work and that impact hinges on additional validation.

Uncertainty about sensitivity to upstream tools: the extent to which POS/lemma/parse errors on learner data drive misclassification is unquantified.

human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The paper presents a deterministic pipeline that combines a linguistically-enhanced alignment with a rule-based classifier (driven by POS/lemma/stem/parse/non-word signals) to auto-annotate GEC system outputs and gold references, enabling fixed-span edit matching and fine-grained per-error-type evaluation. The authors apply the pipeline to CoNLL-2014 outputs, validate label appropriateness via a 200-edit expert rating (reporting aggregated Good+Acceptable ≈ 96.3% and per-rater Good+Acceptable ≥ 95%), and report that reprocessing gold references produces no significant team-level differences in F0.5 under a reported bootstrap test.

Strengths:
- Coherent, modular design separating extraction, classification, and evaluation; practical for auditing and reuse.
- Applied at scale: first comprehensive per-error-type analyses across CoNLL-2014 systems with interpretable diagnostics (operation tiers, POS/morph categories, multi-token analysis, detection vs correction).
- Deterministic rule-based labels increase transparency and enable tracing of decisions; conditional human ratings support label appropriateness when spans are reasonable.

Limitations:
- End-to-end per-category accuracy is not measured: manual validation ignores boundaries, so combined span+label correctness across the full taxonomy (including rare and multi-token types) remains unknown.
- Bootstrap equivalence reporting is underspecified: no CI, resampling unit, per-team/per-category p-values, or multiple-comparison handling are provided, weakening claims of interchangeability with gold for fine-grained evaluation.
- Sensitivity to upstream automatic markup (POS/lemma/parse/stem/non-word detection) is not empirically quantified; authors note POS tagger errors underlie many 'Bad' cases but provide no ablation with alternative taggers or oracle tags.
- Potential extractor-system interaction (merge/split heuristics) may bias per-system/per-type comparisons and is not quantified.

Open Questions:
1) Provide per-error-type extraction precision/recall/F1 and combined span+label agreement (with confusion matrices) from a stratified manual audit including rare and multi-token categories. 2) Fully specify the bootstrap procedure: what was resampled, what statistic(s) were tested, and what per-team/per-category CIs/p-values and corrections were obtained? 3) How robust are labels to alternative tagging pipelines—please rerun with at least one different POS/lemma/parse tool or report oracle-tag bounds. 4) Quantify per-system extraction behavior (split/merge/boundary mismatch rates) and show whether main per-type findings persist under alternative extraction parameters.

Transparency:
Manuscript lists taxonomy, Appendix A (valid combinations), and external-tool versions (spaCy v1.6, Lancaster, Hunspell). Missing are the full rule set (decision logic and priority), exact alignment/merging parameterization, bootstrap code/seed and exact procedure, and processed auto-annotated files and scripts to reproduce tables. Public release of these artifacts is necessary for reproducibility.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident the pipeline is a coherent, practically useful engineering contribution (demonstrated on CoNLL-2014 and supported by conditional human ratings). Confidence is reduced for stronger empirical claims (end-to-end per-type equivalence to gold, dataset-independence across corpora, robustness to tagging/alignment errors) because key validations and reporting details (stratified per-type metrics, bootstrap procedure, ablations) are missing.
